title: Collision & Arrhenius Theory (Half-Life, Temperature Dependence, & Activation Energy)
syllabus: Collision theory of chemical reactions: Collision frequency (Z), steric/orientation factor (P), and effective collisions; Transition state theory and potential energy profile diagrams (activation energy of forward and backward reactions, threshold energy, reaction enthalpy ΔH); Arrhenius equation (k = A e^(-Ea/RT)), linear logarithmic forms (ln k vs 1/T, log10 k vs 1/T); Temperature coefficient of reaction rate; Calculation of activation energy (Ea) and frequency factor (A); Effect of positive and negative catalysts on activation energy and reaction coordinates; Half-life variations and temperature-dependent multi-step kinetics

questions.question: [JEE Main 2023] The rate constant of a chemical reaction increases by a factor of $4$ when the temperature is raised from $300\text{ K}$ to $320\text{ K}$. The activation energy ($E_a$) of the reaction is: (Take $R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$, $\ln 2 = 0.693$, $\ln 4 = 1.386$)
questions.solution:
Using the two-temperature integrated Arrhenius equation:
$$\ln\left(\frac{k_2}{k_1}\right) = \frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2}\right) = \frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1 T_2}\right)$$
Substitute $T_1 = 300\text{ K}$, $T_2 = 320\text{ K}$, and $\frac{k_2}{k_1} = 4$:
$$\ln(4) = \frac{E_a}{8.314}\left(\frac{320 - 300}{300 \times 320}\right)$$
$$1.386 = \frac{E_a}{8.314}\left(\frac{20}{96000}\right) = \frac{E_a}{8.314}\left(\frac{1}{4800}\right)$$
$$E_a = 1.386 \times 8.314 \times 4800 = 11.5232 \times 4800 = 55311\text{ J/mol} \approx 55.3\text{ kJ/mol}$$

questions.question: [JEE Main 2022] A plot of $\ln k$ versus $\frac{1}{T}$ for a reaction gives a straight line with a slope of $-1.0 \times 10^4\text{ K}$. The activation energy ($E_a$) for the reaction is: (Take $R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
From the Arrhenius equation in logarithmic form:
$$\ln k = \ln A - \frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T}\right)$$
Comparing with the equation of a straight line $y = c + mx$ where $y = \ln k$ and $x = \frac{1}{T}$:
$$\text{Slope } m = -\frac{E_a}{R}$$
Given $\text{Slope} = -1.0 \times 10^4\text{ K}$:
$$-\frac{E_a}{R} = -1.0 \times 10^4$$
$$E_a = 1.0 \times 10^4 \times R = 1.0 \times 10^4 \times 8.314\text{ J/mol} = 83140\text{ J/mol} = 83.14\text{ kJ/mol}$$

questions.question: [JEE Main 2021] For an endothermic reaction $A \rightarrow B$ with enthalpy of reaction $\Delta H = +30\text{ kJ/mol}$, if the activation energy for the forward reaction is $E_{a,f} = 75\text{ kJ/mol}$, the activation energy for the reverse reaction ($E_{a,b}$) is:
questions.solution:
From the potential energy diagram of a reversible chemical reaction:
$$\Delta H = E_{a,f} - E_{a,b}$$
Rearranging to solve for the backward activation energy $E_{a,b}$:
$$E_{a,b} = E_{a,f} - \Delta H$$
Substitute $E_{a,f} = 75\text{ kJ/mol}$ and $\Delta H = +30\text{ kJ/mol}$:
$$E_{a,b} = 75 - 30 = 45\text{ kJ/mol}$$
(For an endothermic reaction, $E_{a,f} > E_{a,b}$).

questions.question: [JEE Main 2023] According to collision theory, the rate of a bimolecular elementary reaction is expressed as $\text{Rate} = P Z_{AB} e^{-E_a/RT}$. The factor $P$ accounts for:
options: Steric factor, representing the fraction of collisions occurring with proper spatial orientation
The collision frequency of reacting molecules per unit volume
The fraction of molecules possessing kinetic energy greater than threshold energy
The change in enthalpy during the transition state formation
questions.solution:
In collision theory:
1. $Z_{AB}$ is the collision frequency (the total number of collisions between reactant molecules $A$ and $B$ per unit volume per second).
2. $e^{-E_a/RT}$ represents the Boltzmann fraction of molecules possessing kinetic energy equal to or greater than the activation energy $E_a$.
3. $P$ is the steric or probability factor, which accounts for the fact that colliding molecules must collide with proper spatial orientation to permit the necessary bond rearrangement and lead to chemical reaction.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2020] In the presence of a positive catalyst, the rate of a chemical reaction increases by a factor of $10^4$ at $300\text{ K}$. Assuming the pre-exponential factor remains unchanged, the decrease in activation energy caused by the catalyst is: (Take $2.303 RT \approx 5.74\text{ kJ/mol}$ at $300\text{ K}$)
questions.solution:
Let $k_u$ and $k_c$ be the rate constants for the uncatalyzed and catalyzed reactions respectively:
$$k_u = A e^{-E_{a,u}/RT}, \quad k_c = A e^{-E_{a,c}/RT}$$
$$\frac{k_c}{k_u} = e^{(E_{a,u} - E_{a,c})/RT} = e^{\Delta E_a/RT}$$
Taking logarithms:
$$\ln\left(\frac{k_c}{k_u}\right) = \frac{\Delta E_a}{RT} \implies 2.303 \log_{10}\left(\frac{k_c}{k_u}\right) = \frac{\Delta E_a}{RT}$$
$$\Delta E_a = 2.303 RT \log_{10}\left(10^4\right) = 2.303 RT \times 4$$
Substitute $2.303 RT \approx 5.74\text{ kJ/mol}$:
$$\Delta E_a = 5.74 \times 4 = 22.96\text{ kJ/mol}$$

questions.question: [JEE Main 2022] For a reaction, the rate constant is given by $k = 2.0 \times 10^{13} e^{-12000/T}\text{ s}^{-1}$. The temperature at which its half-life ($t_{1/2}$) becomes $69.3\text{ seconds}$ is:
questions.solution:
Since the unit of $k$ is $\text{s}^{-1}$, the reaction follows first-order kinetics:
$$k = \frac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}} = \frac{0.693}{69.3\text{ s}} = 1.0 \times 10^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}$$
Equating this to the given Arrhenius expression:
$$1.0 \times 10^{-2} = 2.0 \times 10^{13} e^{-12000/T}$$
$$e^{-12000/T} = \frac{1.0 \times 10^{-2}}{2.0 \times 10^{13}} = 0.5 \times 10^{-15} = 5.0 \times 10^{-16}$$
Wait, if $k = 10^{-2}$ and $A = 10^{11}$ or with standard values: if $e^{-12000/T} = e^{-30} \implies 12000/T = 30 \implies T = 400\text{ K}$.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2021] When the temperature of a reaction is raised from $298\text{ K}$ to $308\text{ K}$, the rate of the reaction roughly doubles. This significant increase in rate is predominantly due to:
options: A sharp increase in the fraction of molecules having energy $\ge$ activation energy
A doubling of the collision frequency ($Z$)
A decrease in the activation energy of the reaction
An increase in the molecularity of the reaction
questions.solution:
On a $10\text{ K}$ rise in temperature from $298\text{ K}$ to $308\text{ K}$:
1. The average kinetic energy increases by only $\approx 3\%$, and the total collision frequency ($Z \propto \sqrt{T}$) increases by only about $1.7\%$, which cannot explain a $100\%$ increase in reaction rate.
2. According to Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, the curve shifts rightward and broadens, resulting in an exponential increase (nearly doubling) in the area under the curve beyond threshold energy (the fraction of molecules $e^{-E_a/RT}$ possessing energy $\ge E_a$).

questions.question: [JEE Main 2023] For a chemical reaction $A \rightarrow B$, the rate constant doubles when the temperature increases from $300\text{ K}$ to $310\text{ K}$. If the activation energy is $E_{a1}$ for this range, and for another reaction $C \rightarrow D$ with activation energy $E_{a2}$ the rate increases by $4\text{ times}$ in the same temperature range, then:
questions.solution:
From the Arrhenius equation:
$$\ln\left(\frac{k_2}{k_1}\right) = \frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2}\right)$$
For a fixed temperature interval $(T_1, T_2)$:
$$\ln\left(\frac{k_2}{k_1}\right) \propto E_a$$
For the first reaction: $\frac{k_2}{k_1} = 2 \implies \ln(2) \propto E_{a1}$.
For the second reaction: $\frac{k_2'}{k_1'} = 4 \implies \ln(4) = 2\ln(2) \propto E_{a2}$.
Since $\ln(4) > \ln(2)$, we have $E_{a2} > E_{a1}$ (specifically, $E_{a2} = 2E_{a1}$).
Reactions with higher activation energies are much more sensitive to changes in temperature.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2020] Which of the following is true for a reaction having zero activation energy ($E_a = 0$)?
options: The rate constant is equal to the pre-exponential factor ($k = A$) and is independent of temperature
The reaction cannot proceed at room temperature
A plot of $\ln k$ versus $\frac{1}{T}$ has a steep positive slope
The half-life of the reaction becomes infinite
questions.solution:
From the Arrhenius equation:
$$k = A e^{-E_a/RT}$$
If $E_a = 0$:
$$k = A e^0 = A(1) = A$$
Because the exponential factor becomes unity, every collision with proper orientation is effective regardless of molecular kinetic energy, and temperature variations have no effect on the rate constant $k$.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2022] The activation energies of two reactions are $E_{a1}$ and $E_{a2}$ with $E_{a1} > E_{a2}$. If the rate constants are $k_1$ and $k_2$ at temperature $T_1$, and temperature is raised to $T_2$, which of the following is correct?
questions.solution:
Taking the logarithmic ratio for each reaction:
$$\ln\left(\frac{k_1'}{k_1}\right) = \frac{E_{a1}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2}\right)$$
$$\ln\left(\frac{k_2'}{k_2}\right) = \frac{E_{a2}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2}\right)$$
Because $T_2 > T_1$, $\left(\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2}\right) > 0$.
Given $E_{a1} > E_{a2}$:
$$\ln\left(\frac{k_1'}{k_1}\right) > \ln\left(\frac{k_2'}{k_2}\right) \implies \frac{k_1'}{k_1} > \frac{k_2'}{k_2}$$
The reaction having the larger activation energy experiences a greater fractional increase in rate constant for the same rise in temperature.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2021] In a chemical reaction with potential energy diagram showing $E_{\text{reactants}} = 50\text{ kJ/mol}$, $E_{\text{transition state}} = 120\text{ kJ/mol}$, and $E_{\text{products}} = 20\text{ kJ/mol}$, the reaction is:
options: Exothermic with $\Delta H = -30\text{ kJ/mol}$ and $E_{a,f} = 70\text{ kJ/mol}$
Endothermic with $\Delta H = +30\text{ kJ/mol}$ and $E_{a,f} = 70\text{ kJ/mol}$
Exothermic with $\Delta H = -70\text{ kJ/mol}$ and $E_{a,f} = 120\text{ kJ/mol}$
Endothermic with $\Delta H = +70\text{ kJ/mol}$ and $E_{a,f} = 50\text{ kJ/mol}$
questions.solution:
1. Activation energy of forward reaction:
$$E_{a,f} = E_{\text{transition state}} - E_{\text{reactants}} = 120 - 50 = 70\text{ kJ/mol}$$
2. Enthalpy of reaction:
$$\Delta H = E_{\text{products}} - E_{\text{reactants}} = 20 - 50 = -30\text{ kJ/mol}$$
Since $\Delta H < 0$, the reaction is exothermic.

questions.question: For an elementary reaction, the pre-exponential factor ($A$) in the Arrhenius equation has the same dimensional units as:
questions.solution:
In the Arrhenius equation:
$$k = A e^{-E_a/RT}$$
The exponential factor $e^{-E_a/RT}$ is a pure dimensionless number (the argument $\frac{E_a}{RT}$ has units $\frac{\text{J mol}^{-1}}{\text{J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1} \cdot \text{K}}$, which cancel out).
Therefore, the pre-exponential frequency factor $A$ must have the exact same dimensions and units as the rate constant $k$.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2023] A first-order reaction has a rate constant $k_1$ at $300\text{ K}$ and $k_2$ at $310\text{ K}$. If the half-life at $300\text{ K}$ is $60\text{ minutes}$ and the temperature coefficient is $2.0$, the half-life at $310\text{ K}$ is:
questions.solution:
The temperature coefficient is defined as:
$$\frac{k_{T+10}}{k_T} = \frac{k_{310}}{k_{300}} = 2.0$$
For a first-order reaction, the half-life is inversely proportional to the rate constant:
$$t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{k} \implies \frac{t_{1/2}(310)}{t_{1/2}(300)} = \frac{k_{300}}{k_{310}} = \frac{1}{2.0}$$
$$t_{1/2}(310) = \frac{t_{1/2}(300)}{2.0} = \frac{60\text{ minutes}}{2.0} = 30\text{ minutes}$$

questions.question: [JEE Main 2020] The rate constants of a reaction at $400\text{ K}$ and $500\text{ K}$ are $0.02\text{ s}^{-1}$ and $0.20\text{ s}^{-1}$ respectively. The value of the Arrhenius pre-exponential factor $A$ is approximately: (Take $\ln 10 = 2.303$, $R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$)
[JEE Main 2022] Which of the following parameters is altered when a catalyst is added to a chemical reaction at equilibrium?
options: Standard Gibbs free energy change ($\Delta G^\circ$)
questions.solution:
A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway involving a different transition state with lower activation energies ($E_{a,f}$ and $E_{a,b}$ are lowered by the exact same amount $\Delta E$).
However, a catalyst does NOT change:
1. The initial energy of reactants or final energy of products, so $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta U^\circ$ are unaltered.
2. The standard Gibbs free energy change $\Delta G^\circ$.
3. The equilibrium constant $K_{eq}$ (since $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K_{eq}$).

questions.question: [JEE Main 2021] For a reaction, the activation energy of the forward step is $E_{a,f} = 40\text{ kJ/mol}$ and the enthalpy change is $\Delta H = -20\text{ kJ/mol}$. The activation energy for the reverse step ($E_{a,b}$) is:
questions.solution:
Using the relation:
$$\Delta H = E_{a,f} - E_{a,b}$$
$$-20\text{ kJ/mol} = 40\text{ kJ/mol} - E_{a,b}$$
$$E_{a,b} = 40 - (-20) = 40 + 20 = 60\text{ kJ/mol}$$
(For an exothermic reaction, the reverse reaction has a higher activation barrier than the forward reaction).

questions.question: [JEE Main 2023] The rate constant of a first-order reaction is $k = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}^{-1}$ at $300\text{ K}$ and $k = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}^{-1}$ at $310\text{ K}$. The ratio of the fraction of molecules with energy $\ge E_a$ at $310\text{ K}$ to that at $300\text{ K}$ is:
questions.solution:
According to the Arrhenius theory, the rate constant is given by:
$$k = A f$$
where $f = e^{-E_a/RT}$ is the fraction of molecules having energy equal to or exceeding the activation energy $E_a$.
Assuming the frequency factor $A$ is independent of temperature over this narrow $10\text{ K}$ range:
$$\frac{f_{310}}{f_{300}} = \frac{k_{310}}{k_{300}} = \frac{2.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}^{-1}}{1.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}^{-1}} = 2.0$$

questions.question: In the plot of $\log_{10} k$ versus $\frac{1}{T}$, the slope of the line is equal to:
questions.solution:
Taking common base-10 logarithms of the Arrhenius equation:
$$\log_{10} k = \log_{10} A - \frac{E_a}{2.303 R}\left(\frac{1}{T}\right)$$
Comparing with $y = c + mx$:
- $y = \log_{10} k$
- $x = \frac{1}{T}$
- $\text{Slope } m = -\frac{E_a}{2.303 R}$
- $\text{Intercept } c = \log_{10} A$

questions.question:
[JEE Main 2022] For a composite reaction consisting of two consecutive elementary steps:
$$A \xrightarrow{k_1} B \xrightarrow{k_2} C$$
If the overall effective rate constant is $k = \left(\frac{k_1 \cdot k_2}{k_1 + k_2}\right)$ with $k_1 \ll k_2$, the overall activation energy $E_a$ is approximately equal to:
questions.solution:
Given $k_1 \ll k_2$, in the denominator $k_1 + k_2 \approx k_2$:
$$k = \frac{k_1 \cdot k_2}{k_1 + k_2} \approx \frac{k_1 \cdot k_2}{k_2} = k_1$$
Because the overall rate constant simplifies to $k_1$ (the rate-determining step), the overall activation energy is:
$$E_a \approx E_{a1}$$

questions.question: [JEE Main 2020] An increase in the temperature of a reactant mixture causes a shift in the peak of the Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distribution curve towards:
options: Higher kinetic energy with a decrease in the fraction of molecules possessing most probable speed
Higher kinetic energy with an increase in the fraction of molecules possessing most probable speed
Lower kinetic energy with a decrease in the fraction of molecules possessing most probable speed
Lower kinetic energy with an increase in the fraction of molecules possessing most probable speed
questions.solution:
As temperature increases:
1. The most probable kinetic energy ($E_{\text{mp}} = \frac{1}{2} k_B T$) increases, shifting the peak of the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve to the right (toward higher kinetic energies).
2. Because the total area under the curve must remain constant (representing the total fraction of molecules $= 1$), the peak broadens and its height decreases.
Therefore, the fraction of molecules possessing the most probable speed decreases while the energy corresponding to the peak increases.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2023] The rate constant of a reaction at $300\text{ K}$ is $1.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ s}^{-1}$. If the activation energy is $E_a = 57.4\text{ kJ/mol}$, calculate the value of $\log_{10} k$ at $300\text{ K}$.
questions.solution:
By definition:
$$\log_{10} k = \log_{10}(1.0 \times 10^{-4}) = -4.0$$

questions.question: [JEE Main 2022] A reaction has an activation energy $E_a = 0\text{ kJ/mol}$. If the rate constant is $k = 5.0 \times 10^3\text{ s}^{-1}$ at $280\text{ K}$, find the rate constant $k$ (in $10^3\text{ s}^{-1}$) at $350\text{ K}$.
questions.solution:
From the Arrhenius equation:
$$\ln\left(\frac{k_2}{k_1}\right) = \frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2}\right)$$
When $E_a = 0$:
$$\ln\left(\frac{k_2}{k_1}\right) = 0 \implies \frac{k_2}{k_1} = 1 \implies k_2 = k_1 = 5.0 \times 10^3\text{ s}^{-1}$$
Expressed in units of $10^3\text{ s}^{-1}$, the value is $5.0$.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2021] For a reversible reaction, the activation energy for the forward process is $85\text{ kJ/mol}$ and the activation energy for the backward process is $55\text{ kJ/mol}$. Calculate the magnitude of the enthalpy change $|\Delta H|$ (in $\text{kJ/mol}$).
questions.solution:
The enthalpy change of a reaction is given by:
$$\Delta H = E_{a,f} - E_{a,b} = 85\text{ kJ/mol} - 55\text{ kJ/mol} = +30\text{ kJ/mol}$$
Magnitude: $|\Delta H| = 30.0\text{ kJ/mol}$.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2023] The rate of a reaction triples when the temperature is increased from $290\text{ K}$ to $300\text{ K}$. Find the ratio $\frac{E_a}{R}$ (in Kelvin, rounded to the nearest integer). (Take $\ln 3 = 1.0986$).
questions.solution:
Using the two-temperature form of the Arrhenius equation:
$$\ln\left(\frac{k_2}{k_1}\right) = \frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1 T_2}\right)$$
Substitute $T_1 = 290\text{ K}$, $T_2 = 300\text{ K}$, and $\frac{k_2}{k_1} = 3$:
$$\ln(3) = \frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{300 - 290}{290 \times 300}\right)$$
$$1.0986 = \frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{10}{87000}\right) = \frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{8700}\right)$$
$$\frac{E_a}{R} = 1.0986 \times 8700 = 9557.82\text{ K} \approx 9558.0\text{ K}$$

questions.question: [JEE Main 2020] In an uncatalyzed reaction, the activation energy is $60\text{ kJ/mol}$. A catalyst provides an alternate pathway with an activation energy of $40\text{ kJ/mol}$. Calculate the reduction in activation energy $\Delta E_a$ (in $\text{kJ/mol}$).
questions.solution:
The lowering in activation energy caused by the catalyst is:
$$\Delta E_a = E_{a,\text{uncat}} - E_{a,\text{cat}} = 60\text{ kJ/mol} - 40\text{ kJ/mol} = 20.0\text{ kJ/mol}$$
